name: Bianca Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. We don't sell or campaign for a side. Everything here is confidential. What was on your desk this morning?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Bianca Dubois, forty-three, and I lead an accounting firm's arts-venue accounts and tax-return work. This morning I traced a lighting grant to the theatre's old contract; I like turning a tangle of restrictions into a sentence a manager can use. I dislike rushing out a draft that leaves the manager with no one to call. I'm one of our strongest accountants, with a master's degree and a chartered accountancy qualification.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What are your tools and home life like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I use an AI note tool now and then after the tax partners have tested it, then check the output myself. My husband Leo repairs bicycles, and our children are nine and twelve; we have a mortgage and about five months of expenses saved. My pay is typical for a senior accountant, and some similar firms are nearby. I'm willing to change a routine when a colleague can show me it works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would still spend Monday closing the arts venues' accounts. Our firm sometimes uses an AI note tool after the tax partners have tested it, but the signed return and its explanation still come to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team to use the note tool only for a first draft and check the grant figures against the contract. I'd tell the theatre manager I will remain the person who answers a question about the accounts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My pay is about normal for a senior accountant, and Leo and I have five months of expenses saved. I don't love a new system on day one, but I can use it once a colleague has shown the checks. Some local firms do similar work, so a small tool is not a threat to our whole household.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep leading the venue-account closing rota and use the tested note tool for meeting notes now and then. At our next client review I'd ask where the draft notes have saved time and where they have missed a figure. I would keep our mortgage and savings payments at their current levels unless the pay or work actually changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. The work I enjoy and our household money both look steady in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did you explain at breakfast?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At breakfast my younger child asked why the theatre can spend grant money on lighting but not on the heating bill. I used the same contract clause I had explained to its manager. I like when an accounting rule becomes a sentence someone can use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge the note tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare the draft note's grant amounts and dates with the contract before it goes anywhere. We do not need to spend our reserve to buy into a note tool the firm already pays for.

say: I would use **checked draft notes** for meeting records without changing who signs the accounts.
I would remain the **named accountant** for venue questions.
think: Our **five-month reserve** and typical pay make the current work feel steady.
I trust **tested tools** only after checking their errors.
do: Continue **venue accounts** and occasional tested AI notes with human sign-off.
Review **missed grant figures** at the next client meeting.
feel: I feel **calm** about work and household money.
S0.quote: I like when an accounting rule becomes a sentence someone can use.
fieldNote: Her **current occasional AI use** is an established routine, not a new learning action.
Typical **senior pay**, five months saved and some nearby firms make the plateau feel secure.

steps.text: Keep closing venue accounts with occasional tested AI notes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tool could write client replies and produce first accounts drafts, which are a lot of billable hours. I would expect the partners to remove a reviewer day before they remove the promise of a quick turnaround.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the partners to show us the fee and staffing numbers before changing the rota. I'd tell clients the fast draft still needs a real answer when a restricted grant causes a dispute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own Friday review day might be cut, so my pay could shrink. Five months saved would let us adjust, but Leo's bicycle-shop wage alone would not carry the mortgage and two children. I use AI now and then after others test it, yet I won't assume it creates enough new fees to protect my post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put six weeks of draft errors and client questions beside the proposed new rota at our December meeting. I'd keep the paid Friday reviews while they exist and ask for a written decision on my hours. If the day is cut, I'd apply for an advertised arts centre finance manager post only after written mortgage-covering pay, start and school pickup are confirmed; if the posting closes, I'd stay employed and watch the next one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a possible cut to my wage. The reserve buys time to look, not permission to ignore the payslip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Friday pickup require?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our nine-year-old finishes school at three, and Leo works late at the bike shop on Fridays. I would need a confirmed after-school club place before taking an arts centre role with late closing. Its cost would have to fit the written net pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you count besides saved minutes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some venue clients call after reading the draft because their grant rules are unusual. I'd count those calls, not only the minutes saved by the software. If a manager says the role is coming but cannot show a posting, I'd keep the job I have.

say: I would show **draft errors** beside staffing savings.
I would ask for **written paid hours** before a rota cut.
think: My **Friday wage** could shrink if the firm removes a paid review day.
Leo’s **shop wage** cannot carry the mortgage alone.
do: Compare **six weeks of errors** with the new rota.
After **hours cuts**, apply only for posted work with written mortgage pay, start and club.
feel: I feel **anxious** about possible pay loss.
S1.quote: The reserve buys time to look, not permission to ignore the payslip.
fieldNote: The **own-Friday risk** justifies anxiety despite five months saved and nearby employers.
An **arts centre move** requires an advertised funded vacancy, written mortgage pay, firm start and confirmed club cost.

steps.text: Compare six-week error log with proposed rota while keeping offered paid Friday reviews

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2028 could prepare the venue accounts, tax returns and grant explanations I spend the week on. Robots around 2031 arrive after the thinking work, so they do not give my desk another three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the partners for written notice and real paid openings before making anyone redundant. I'd tell my family that we can postpone purchases while we protect the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the firm could end my accounting post in the first year after 2028. Our five-month reserve is helpful, but Leo's repair-shop wage cannot carry the mortgage and both children for long. A strong chartered accountant can still lose a desk job when the desk work becomes cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pause the one-time living-room sofa order costing seven hundred and leave that cash in savings. While still employed, I'd check actual postings at the arts centre and venue operators. If my post ends in the first year after AGI arrives in 2028, I'd claim temporary income support and accept a funded on-site operations role only with written mortgage-covering net pay, a confirmed start and Friday club cost covered; without one, I'd keep any paid accounting hours and search each week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Five months gives us a bridge, but not a second career already built.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leo and I would tell the children the sofa can wait and school stays as it is. I would call the after-school club before accepting any late venue hours. An unconfirmed after-school club place is not a childcare plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the venue manager offers only encouragement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A venue manager might like my experience, but that is not a funded vacancy. I would keep taking paid accounts files while the firm offers them, until a written start and wage are in front of me. I would file the income support claim promptly after a formal end date.

say: I would demand **written notice** and real paid openings before redundancies.
I would protect the **mortgage** before buying furniture.
think: My **accounting post** may end in the first year after AGI arrives in 2028.
Our **five-month reserve** cannot replace my wage indefinitely.
do: Pause the **one-time sofa order** and hold seven hundred.
After **2028 post loss**, claim support and seek funded venue work.
Keep **paid files if offered** until written mortgage pay, start and club costs fit.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about expected post loss.
S2.quote: An unconfirmed after-school club place is not a childcare plan.
fieldNote: **AGI by 2028** reaches her thinking work first; later robots do not extend the accounting deadline.
Her **venue route** requires a funded posted role, written net mortgage pay, start and confirmed Friday club costs.

steps.text: Pause one-time sofa order and hold seven hundred in savings
Claim temporary income support after 2028 post loss
Check posted venue vacancies now; move after loss with written net mortgage pay, start and club
Keep offered paid accounting files while no funded venue opening fits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to learn the on-site side of running a venue instead of being only the person who files its accounts. AGI in 2031 still reaches my tax desk, and robots around 2034 come later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the partners and a venue client for paid shadowing on an event night. I'd tell my team a new skill needs a schedule and supervisor, not a brochure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know the budgets but not the door, safety or staffing work. My five months of savings should stay for the mortgage, so I would only train while earning. A venue manager might prefer someone with direct operations experience, which is why I want real supervised shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This spring I'd ask the arts centre for four supervised paid event shifts and my firm for paid release on those evenings. If both approve, I'd work those shifts and learn the safety and staffing routines; if either refuses, I'd keep paid accounts work and ask again at the next venue. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, if my tax post ends, I'd apply for a posted funded venue operations job only with written mortgage-covering net pay, a start and confirmed Friday club; if none fits, I'd claim income support if eligible and take any paid firm hours still offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but five years lets me learn the floor work while still drawing a wage. I won't buy a new title with our mortgage reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the duty manager do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the last arts centre fundraiser I watched the duty manager move volunteers when the entry queue backed up. I knew its budget, but I did not know how to keep that doorway safe. I want a supervisor to show me on a real shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take unpaid shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the firm will not release me on pay, I will not disappear for four unpaid evenings. I would keep the venue accounts and ask the next client about a funded shift. A shadowing offer with no actual supervisor is not enough.

S3.quote: I won't buy a new title with our mortgage reserve.
fieldNote: The **four-shift plan** is actual paid supervised learning, conditional on venue pay and firm release.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years could let me work enough real venue shifts to decide whether I want that life, and build the reserve past five months. AGI in 2036 still reaches my accounting desk before robots around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues to ask for paid transition time well before the final tax season. I'd ask venue managers to describe actual roles and wages, not say their doors are always open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2036 our children would be nineteen and twenty-two, so Friday school club would no longer be the issue. I would not rely on either child's wage to pay our mortgage. An operations role might suit me, but I need a funded vacancy and written pay, not ten years of friendly conversations.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next year I'd seek four supervised paid event shifts with approved paid firm release; if the approvals fail, I'd keep my accounting salary. I'd transfer eighty a month into savings while Leo and I both retain current pay, stopping if either wage falls. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, if my tax post ends, I'd take only a posted funded venue operations role with written mortgage-covering net pay and a fixed start; if none exists, I'd claim support if eligible and take any paid accounting work still offered while looking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than terrified, because the longer runway and five-month reserve give me choices. A venue role still has to exist when I need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the children need pickup in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children would be nineteen and twenty-two in 2036, so school pickup would no longer control the job decision. Leo and I can put eighty aside from the present budget without borrowing from the mortgage account. We will review it after each school year as the children grow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no venue vacancy appears?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the arts centre has no post in 2036, I would check other posted venue openings and keep any firm hours I can. I would not take a volunteer role and call it an income plan. The start date and pay would still have to be in writing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because it could end my accounting wage before I learn the on-site venue work properly. Five months saved buys a little time, but Leo's bicycle-shop pay cannot carry our mortgage for long. Paid supervised shifts, written notice and a funded opening with clear pay and a start would help. A friendly venue manager is not a posted job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who trains the person who keeps an event safe after software has finished the budget. I know the grant numbers, but I would need to learn the door and staffing routines from a real supervisor. That is work worth paying for.

headlineQuote: A friendly venue manager is not a posted job.
portrait: At **forty-three**, Bianca leads arts-venue accounts and tax returns.
Her **master’s** and chartered qualification support top skill and typical senior pay.
She uses **AI occasionally** after testing and checks each draft.
Leo’s **bicycle-shop wage**, two children, mortgage and five-month reserve shape her choices.
Some **nearby firms** offer options, but she tests paid on-site venue work before changing jobs.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her accounting wage before she learns venue operations.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **paid supervised shifts**, written notice and a funded opening with real pay and start.
